brief: JPMorgan's Andrew Tyler frames the November midterms as a Senate trade. Betting markets give Democrats an 85% chance of taking the House, leaving no edge there, while Kalshi puts a Republican Senate hold at 53%. Base rates across 23 cycles since 1934, roughly 27 House seats and 3 Senate seats lost by the president's party, applied to a 218-seat Republican House and a 53-47 Senate, imply the same split. Six races decide the Senate and Democrats need four flips. The bank's implied probabilities favor Democrats in exactly four: North Carolina 91%, Maine 69%, Alaska 65%, Ohio 54%, against Iowa at 62% Republican and Texas a toss-up. The D1 desk prices three basket pairs off Kalshi joint outcomes of 47% Democratic Congress, 39% split, 16% Republican sweep. The Democratic pair is long ACA-exposed managed care and low-income consumer, short small and mid-cap defense, capital markets, energy permitting and CLARITY Act names. The Republican pair mirrors it. The split pair keeps ACA and defense primes long and shorts capital markets on rising oversight. Lakos-Bujas adds that divided government coincided with 20% two-year S&P 500 returns since 1950 against 18% under single-party control, and veto plus filibuster blunt even a sweep.
